cues: Then his mother mentions Runtu, who always asks after him.
At that name a picture flashes into his mind: the golden moon, the watermelons, the boy with the pitchfork.
Thirty years ago, when the family was still rich, Runtu, the son of a part time labourer, came to help guard the ritual vessels at a great sacrifice.
He wore a silver necklet, because his father had pledged him to the gods.
Within hours the two boys were fast friends.
Runtu knew wonders: how to trap birds in the snow, where to find shells of every colour, fish that jumped on two legs.
The town boys, by contrast, only ever saw the four corners of sky above their courtyard wall.
